response: Yes, ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) can affect the neurological outcome after traumatic cervical cord injury. OPLL is a condition where the posterior longitudinal ligament in the spine becomes calcified, which can narrow the spinal canal and put pressure on the spinal cord. In the event of a traumatic cervical cord injury, the presence of OPLL can worsen the injury and lead to a poorer neurological outcome due to the increased pressure on the spinal cord and reduced space for the cord to expand. Studies have shown that patients with OPLL who suffer a traumatic cervical cord injury tend to have more severe neurological deficits and a lower likelihood of recovery compared to those without OPLL.
